title: The Update Your VP Can Act On
promise: Turn a status update into a clear business outcome, recommendation and decision.
hook: Your VP replies: ‘So what do you need from me?’
intro: You may have done valuable work. But a list of completed tasks makes the reader do the work of finding its value. A useful update connects what changed to why it matters and what should happen next.
quick: Take the last update you sent. Underline the sentence that says what changed for the business or customer. If you cannot find one, that is the sentence to write first.
inside: A four-part structure you can reuse

examples.label: Technology
examples.before: We migrated 11 services and closed 42 tickets.
examples.after: Checkout failures fell from 8% to 3% in the week after the fix. That is five fewer failed attempts per 100. Traffic mix may explain part of the change. I recommend monitoring for another week before extending the rollout. Please approve holding the next release until Friday.
examples.why: Name the observed change, keep uncertainty visible, and ask for a specific decision. Do not label the change as revenue earned without evidence.

examples.label: Operations
examples.before: We held training for all three shifts.
examples.after: Picking errors fell from 12 to 7 per 1,000 orders during the two-week pilot on shift A. We have not tested the other shifts. I recommend extending the pilot to shift B. Can you release two trainer hours next Tuesday?
examples.why: The denominator and period make the result interpretable. The next step is bounded.

examples.label: Commercial
examples.before: We met six customers and updated the sales deck.
examples.after: Four of six renewal conversations raised onboarding delays. I recommend testing a named onboarding owner on the next three renewals. This is a small sample, not proof of a market-wide issue. Can Sales and Operations agree an owner by Thursday?
examples.why: A qualitative signal is useful when you explain its limits. You do not need to manufacture a metric.

method: 1. Lead with the change
Say what is different for the customer, cost, risk, time or capacity. If the outcome is not known, say what you learned or what remains blocked.
2. Show enough evidence
Include a period, a comparison and a source. Separate observed change from your explanation of what caused it. Use plain language.
3. Make a recommendation
Propose one next step. Say what it would protect or improve, and what it would delay, cost or put at risk.
4. Make the request explicit
Name the decision, owner and deadline. If no decision is needed, say ‘For awareness; next review Friday.’ Do not create an approval request for work you already own.
script: Since [date], [outcome] changed from [baseline] to [current state]. This matters because [business effect]. We still need to check [uncertainty]. I recommend [action]. I need [decision or support] from [person] by [date].
worksheetIntro: Use a recent piece of work. Keep customer names, internal figures and confidential details on your own copy.
prompts: My original update
What changed, for whom, and over what period?
What evidence supports it? What remains uncertain?
What do I recommend, and what is the trade-off?
What do I need, from whom and by when?
My rewritten update in four sentences
checks: The first sentence describes an outcome, learning or obstacle.
Any number has a meaningful baseline, unit and time period.
I have not claimed sole credit for a team outcome.
My recommendation and request are easy to find.
experiment: Use the rewrite in your next update. After the conversation, note the first question you were asked. Did it move to the decision, or did the reader still need to reconstruct the context? Use that question to improve the next update.
reflection: What did the reader understand faster? What did I still need to explain?
nextTitle: See where your impact gets lost.
nextText: The Leadership Visibility Check gives you six situations to practice explaining outcomes, making the main point clear and reducing uncertainty.

title: ‘Be More Strategic’: What to Do in Your Next Meeting
promise: Translate vague feedback into a recommendation, a trade-off and a decision people can make.
hook: ‘Be more strategic’ is feedback. It is not an instruction.
intro: In your next meeting, make the choice clearer. Show what matters, what cannot all happen at once, and what you recommend. You do not need a bigger presentation to start practicing judgment.
quick: Choose one unresolved decision on your calendar this week. Write ‘We need to decide whether to…’ If your sentence describes a task list, keep going until the choice is visible.
inside: Four ways to respond to vague feedback

examples.label: The situation
examples.before: We will try to deliver both requests this week.
examples.after: The team has 30 hours available. The customer fix needs 20 hours and the internal report needs 20. Doing both needs 40 hours, so we must move scope, time or capacity.
examples.why: The constraint is explicit. Working harder is not an unexplained source of ten extra hours.

examples.label: The recommendation
examples.before: Which one would you like us to prioritize?
examples.after: I recommend the customer fix this week and the full report next week. The fix addresses a current customer issue. The report supports a planning meeting that can move by three days. We can use the remaining ten hours for report preparation. Please confirm the planning meeting can move.
examples.why: You compare consequences, make a choice and name the agreement needed from another team.

examples.label: What could change the answer
examples.after: If the report has a fixed regulatory deadline, the recommendation changes. We would need to narrow the fix or secure ten hours of qualified capacity. I will confirm that constraint with Finance today and review the plan tomorrow.
examples.why: A recommendation becomes more credible when you can explain the evidence that would change it.

methodTitle: Turn four familiar phrases into actions.
method: ‘Be more strategic.’
Connect the choice to a business priority and a time horizon. Explain what the organization gains and what it gives up. Include the option of delaying or doing less.
‘Have executive presence.’
Begin with the recommendation. Then give the two facts that matter most. Pause for questions. Clear thinking and a calm explanation are more useful than performing certainty.
‘Think out of the box.’
Offer a credible different path: a smaller test, a changed sequence or a different constraint. Explain why it could work and how you would test it.
‘Show more ownership.’
Name the next action, owner, decision boundary and review date. Raise an obstacle with a proposed response, rather than waiting for it to become someone else’s surprise.
script: The decision is [choice]. We could [A] or [B]. Given [priority and constraint], I recommend [option]. The trade-off is [cost or delay]. I would change my mind if [evidence]. We will review [measure] on [date].
worksheetIntro: Complete this before the meeting. Aim for a recommendation you can explain in under a minute, with supporting detail ready.
prompts: The decision, its owner and the deadline
The business outcome and the constraint
Two credible options and the consequence of each
My recommendation and the trade-off I accept
What evidence would change my mind?
The agreement I need, next action and review date
checks: This is a decision, not a list of activities.
I have checked the constraints with the people affected.
I can explain why I prefer one credible option.
I have named uncertainty and a way to revisit the decision.
experiment: Bring the completed sheet to one meeting. Start with the recommendation and ask, ‘Which assumption or trade-off do you see differently?’ Record what changed after the discussion. Better judgment includes revising your view when the facts change.
reflection: Which question exposed a missing fact? What will I check before the next meeting?
nextTitle: Practice the choice before the meeting.
nextText: The Senior-Level Judgment Check uses six situations about decisions, priorities and ownership. Use your result to choose a skill to practice next.

title: How Many Months of Choice Do You Have?
promise: Make a first estimate of household runway and identify the alternatives that make it useful.
hook: A large salary and room to choose are different things.
intro: Earning Power is what the market will pay for what you can do and prove. Exit Power includes how long your household can maintain its chosen life without your income, and which acceptable alternatives remain. Start by making the household picture visible.
quick: Gather recent bank statements, recurring bills and annual commitments. Use actual household spending. Keep the numbers on your own copy. You do not need to share them to use this guide.

examples.label: A fictional household
examples.before: We have ₹30 lakh in savings, so we should be fine.
examples.after: Of ₹30 lakh, ₹6 lakh is reserved for a goal the household will not touch. Reachable money available for runway is ₹24 lakh after assumed selling costs and tax. Spending is ₹1.2 lakh a month, including annual bills divided by twelve. If all income stops: ₹24 lakh ÷ ₹1.2 lakh = 20 months.
examples.why: The same money cannot fund both a protected goal and the runway. The example holds spending fixed and assumes no investment returns or inflation.

examples.label: If one income continues
examples.before: Two salaries mean twice the security.
examples.after: Assume ₹60,000 of dependable take-home income continues each month. The monthly gap becomes ₹1.2 lakh minus ₹60,000 = ₹60,000. ₹24 lakh ÷ ₹60,000 = 40 months. If both incomes stop, the original 20-month estimate applies.
examples.why: Continuing income changes the gap. Test whether both incomes depend on the same employer, sector or economic conditions.

examples.label: A different spending scenario
examples.before: We could cut everything if we had to.
examples.after: If the household explicitly agrees a temporary ₹1 lakh monthly budget, all-income-stops runway becomes 24 months. Keep that separate from the 20-month estimate for the current life. Record exactly what would change.
examples.why: An imagined emergency budget is not the same as maintaining the life your household has chosen.

method: A. Reachable, available money

Count money you could access in a week or two and would actually use, after costs and taxes. Exclude your home, unvested shares, locked retirement money and protected goals. Market values can fall; record the valuation date.
B. Actual monthly spending
Include housing, EMIs, school, household costs, transport, support for parents and other commitments. Divide annual bills by twelve. Check statements rather than relying on memory.
C. Continuing net income
For a one-income-stops scenario, count only income you reasonably expect to continue after tax and costs. Do not count a hoped-for bonus, future job or untested business revenue as dependable income.
D. Calculate and stress-test

All income stops: A ÷ B. One income stops: A ÷ (B − C), only if B is greater than C. If C covers B, there is no current monthly gap in this simplified model; that does not mean unlimited security. Recheck under less favorable assumptions.
script: This is a first estimate, not a retirement plan or a recommendation to resign, invest or sell assets. It leaves out future inflation, returns and unexpected costs. Revisit the numbers and use qualified advice for consequential financial decisions.
worksheetIntro: Use one currency throughout. Agree what is available and what is protected with the people whose lives depend on it.
prompts: Date / currency / A: reachable money after protected goals and costs
B: monthly spending, including annual costs ÷ 12
All income stops: A ÷ B = ___ months
C: dependable continuing income / gap B − C / A ÷ gap
What if both incomes stop, costs rise or an asset falls in value?
Two acceptable alternatives, and what would make each real
checks: I have excluded locked, unvested and separately protected money.
I used household spending, including annual commitments.
I have separated current-life and lower-spending scenarios.
I can name an acceptable next move and the work it requires.
experiment: Choose one small action for the next month: reconcile the spending figure, clarify a commitment, test whether an alternative role exists, or speak with someone who understands a path you are considering. Write down who will do it and when you will revisit the picture.
reflection: What could I realistically choose this year? Which assumption most changes that answer?
nextTitle: Explore the choices behind the number.
nextText: The Exit Power Check helps you reflect on financial visibility, flexibility and alternatives. The book develops how Earning Power and Exit Power work together.

title: Passed Over. What Do You Ask Next?
promise: Prepare a useful manager conversation about evidence, expectations and the next opportunity.
hook: ‘Keep doing what you’re doing’ gives you very little to act on.
intro: A missed promotion can leave several questions tangled together: your readiness, the evidence people saw, and whether a role was available. A useful conversation separates them. The goal is clearer information and an agreed next step.
quick: Write down the exact explanation you received. Beside it, write what you inferred. Mark each statement as known, assumed or still to ask. Do this before composing your reply.

examples.label: The opening
examples.before: Why was I passed over when I delivered everything?
examples.after: I want to understand the decision and make the next few months useful. Could we separate my readiness for the scope from the availability of a role? What did the decision makers need to see that they did not see this time?
examples.why: You ask about the decision without assuming that delivery, readiness and role availability are the same question.

examples.label: Make the feedback observable
examples.before: They said I need to be more strategic.
examples.after: Could we look at one recent situation where you wanted different judgment from me? In the regional rollout meeting, what would a stronger recommendation have included? What would have changed the decision?
examples.why: A specific situation gives you something you can practice. A label alone can lead to months of guessing.

examples.label: Agree a next test
examples.before: I will work harder and be ready next time.
examples.after: I can lead the options review for the next rollout. Could we agree which decisions I own, what evidence would show stronger judgment, and who needs to see that work? Let us review it in six weeks. I understand that demonstrating readiness does not guarantee an open role.
examples.why: A bounded assignment, visible evidence and a review date create a useful plan without pretending to control the promotion outcome.

method: 1. What drove this decision?
Was the issue readiness, evidence, sponsorship, role availability or another constraint? Ask what your manager can share; do not request confidential comparisons with a colleague.
2. What specific example shows the gap?
Ask for a recent situation and the response expected at the next level. Repeat the example back to check you understood it.
3. What evidence would change the assessment?
Agree observable behavior and outcomes. ‘Be more visible’ could mean presenting a recommendation to the decision forum, not simply attending more meetings.
4. Where can I demonstrate that?
Identify a real assignment, decision boundaries and necessary support. Confirm what work should stop or move so the assignment is feasible.
5. Who will review it, and when?
Name the reviewer, evidence and date. Ask what remains outside this plan, including vacancies or business conditions.
script: My understanding is [gap], illustrated by [situation]. I will practice it through [assignment], with [support and authority]. We will review [evidence] on [date]. The remaining uncertainty is [role availability or other constraint]. Have I understood that correctly?
worksheetIntro: Use facts you can substantiate. Keep names, performance records and internal decision details private.
prompts: What I was told, in the words used
What I know / what I assumed / what I still need to ask
The most useful specific example to discuss
What evidence would demonstrate readiness?
A feasible assignment, authority and support needed
Reviewer, review date and remaining constraints
checks: I have separated my contribution from the promotion decision.
I have asked for a specific example rather than another label.
The next assignment has realistic scope and support.
The review date and evidence are clear to both of us.
experiment: After the conversation, write a short factual recap and invite corrections. Review the agreed work before the next date. If expectations remain unclear, record that uncertainty rather than inventing a promise. You can then decide what to explore internally or elsewhere with better information.
reflection: What became clearer? What remains unresolved? What choice does that leave me?
nextText: If the conversation is difficult to frame, a free fit call can help you explore whether personal coaching would be useful. Bring an anonymized version of the problem.

title: How to Say No Without Losing Trust
promise: Respond to an unrealistic request with a clear constraint, a useful alternative and an agreed decision.
hook: Every yes spends time that may already belong to something else.
intro: A trustworthy response makes capacity and consequences visible early. You can be helpful without pretending every deadline is possible. The aim is a feasible agreement, while recognizing that you cannot control how another person reacts.
quick: Pick a request you are struggling to accept. Write the requested outcome, deadline and estimated effort. Then name the commitment that would move if you said yes.
inside: A practical way to negotiate scope and timing

examples.label: An impossible deadline
examples.after: I understand you need this for Friday’s decision. The full analysis needs two days; we have one available. I can deliver the two highest-risk scenarios Friday and the full analysis Tuesday. Would the smaller version support Friday’s decision?
examples.why: You acknowledge the purpose, explain the constraint and test a useful alternative. The reduced scope is explicit.

examples.label: A new top priority
examples.before: Sure, we will find a way.
examples.after: We can take this on. It needs about eight hours, which would move the customer review from Thursday to Monday. I recommend protecting the customer review and starting this Friday. If the new request takes priority, can we agree that change with the review owner today?
examples.why: You bring the affected commitment into the conversation before it is missed. You are not quietly making another stakeholder absorb the cost.

examples.label: Work outside the team’s authority
examples.after: I can help frame the issue and share the evidence. The approval sits with Finance, so I cannot commit their budget. Let us take the options to the budget owner. I can prepare the brief by Wednesday.
examples.why: You distinguish help you can offer from authority you do not have. A useful boundary can still move work forward.

methodTitle: Prepare the boundary before the wording.
method: Check the real requirement
Ask what the request enables, when the decision is needed and which parts are essential. A shorter deliverable may solve the actual problem.
Describe capacity concretely
Use available hours, dependencies or existing commitments. An estimate can be a range. Say what you still need to confirm rather than presenting a guess as a fact.
Offer a credible alternative
Change scope, sequence, deadline or qualified capacity. Make sure the alternative is yours to offer. Do not solve one conflict by making an unapproved promise to someone else.
Agree who chooses
If priorities conflict beyond your authority, take the options and consequences to the right decision maker. Confirm what moves, who informs the affected people, and when the plan will be reviewed.
script: I understand the goal is [outcome] by [date]. The constraint is [capacity, dependency or authority]. We can [option A], which means [trade-off], or [option B]. I recommend [choice]. Can [decision owner] confirm by [time]?
worksheetIntro: Use a real, ordinary workplace request. Adapt the wording to your role and relationship; no script guarantees agreement.
prompts: The outcome the requester needs and the deadline
Available capacity, dependencies and decision authority
What would move or suffer if I said yes?
Two feasible alternatives and the consequence of each
My recommendation and the decision owner
The words I will use, plus the follow-up agreement
checks: I understand the outcome behind the request.
The constraint is specific and honest.
My alternative is feasible and within my authority.
Affected people will hear about any changed commitment.
experiment: Use the structure in one low-stakes conversation. Ask the other person which part is essential. Afterward, confirm the agreed scope and date in writing. Check whether the agreement held and what you learned about estimating or communicating the constraint.
reflection: What did we agree to protect? What moved? Did everyone affected know?

title: Before Your Next Review: Capture the Evidence
short: Record the judgment, not just the task.
promise: Turn one recent contribution into a credible story of judgment, impact and shared credit.
hook: At review time, a long task list still leaves the reader asking: ‘So what?’
intro: Useful evidence explains the situation, the choice you made, what changed and how you know. Capture it while the details are fresh. You are building a record someone else can understand and check.
quick: Choose one contribution from the last month. Find the original brief, decision note or result. Start with the record, rather than reconstructing a more flattering story from memory.
inside: Prompts for outcomes that resist easy measurement
A printable evidence sheet for your next review

examples.label: A task list
examples.before: Led the onboarding project. Ran weekly meetings. Created the tracker.
examples.after: New client onboarding had no clear owner between Sales and Operations. I compared a centralized queue with a named owner per client, then proposed a four-week pilot of named owners on eight comparable accounts.
examples.why: The situation and choice reveal your judgment. Meeting frequency alone does not explain your contribution.

examples.label: The observed outcome
examples.after: Median time from signed contract to first usable setup was 12 days for the prior eight comparable accounts and 8 days for the eight pilot accounts. The samples are small and account complexity varied, so the pilot does not prove causation. We have not measured a revenue effect.
examples.why: A baseline, definition, period and limitation make the outcome checkable. Do not claim an unmeasured downstream result.

examples.label: Evidence and shared credit
examples.after: My contribution was framing the options, securing both teams’ agreement and setting the review criteria. Operations ran the pilot and Sales improved the handover data. The signed pilot brief and onboarding log support the record. We agreed a second pilot before wider rollout.
examples.why: You make your own role visible without absorbing the team’s work. The next decision shows how the evidence was used.

method: Describe the stakes
What was at risk or needed to improve? Include scope and constraints. ‘This mattered’ becomes useful when the reader knows to whom and why.
Show the judgment
What did you choose, recommend, negotiate or stop? What was the alternative? Distinguish decisions you owned from decisions you influenced.
Use the evidence you have
A time series, a documented decision, a stakeholder confirmation or a clearer handover can all help. If you have no numeric outcome, describe an observable change and how it was confirmed.
Name limits and shared credit
Record other contributors and uncertainty. Never turn a forecast into a realized saving. If you claim time saved, show the calculation and whether that time was actually redeployed.
script: The situation was [problem and stakes]. I [specific judgment or contribution], choosing [option] over [alternative] because [reason]. We observed [change] over [period], supported by [record]. [People or teams] contributed [work]. We still need to check [limitation].
worksheetIntro: Keep source records in your approved workplace systems. Use references here, not confidential documents copied into personal storage.
prompts: Situation, scope and why it mattered
My decision or contribution, and the alternative considered
What changed, compared with what and over what period?
Evidence location and someone who can confirm it
Other contributors, limitations and what is not yet proven
A concise review-ready version and the next decision
checks: Someone outside the project can understand why it mattered.
My contribution is distinct from the team’s total result.
Every outcome is supported or clearly labeled as an estimate.
The evidence can be checked in an appropriate system.
experiment: Set aside ten minutes each Friday to capture one contribution. Before your review, choose the examples most relevant to the scope you want to demonstrate. Ask your manager what evidence is missing. A record supports a conversation; it does not guarantee a promotion.
reflection: Which example shows a wider scope of judgment? What evidence would make it stronger?
nextTitle: Make the contribution easier to see.
